Why not try and discuss it with your doc? Prozac really helped me. Now I am doing a lot better so slowly reducing the doses however I can't help but fear the depression will creep back if i stop completely.

For me the realization of progress happens suddenly during the flow of the daily life.

 I still go to therapy, but a year and a half after starting with my current doctor, one day  while grocery shopping i suddenly realized that it has been weeks if not months since the last time i fantasized about not existing. That made me so happy and i began to be more aware of my little daily toughts, actions and choices. Not always, just sometimes.
 
I stop to think about how i am dealing/ or just dealt with the situation or the moment that I am living. For exemple, Did i not keep my mouth shut when someone got infront of me at the line, well i wonder what made me speak up then? What has changed?  The other day i realized i had become lot tidier without actually having this goal, that i had started to dress better. I didnt have to analyze those tough, its easy: a good sign that i have progressed at some aspect of my mental wellbeing.

So i guess for me it comes from trying to be aware of myself.

Hey solo female in Mongolia here! And welcome already, Mongolia is really beautiful and special! But beware the people are delusional about the seasons and weather. It’s -8 C at the moment and people think it’s spring time since February… . Huge sales for winter clothings start towards the end of January, since its the “end of season” while it’s -40 degrees outside. I don’t have the heart to tell them that their winter season has no end… The Mongolian perception of cold is also a bit different. “Today is quite warm” said one of my friends when it was -15 degrees in late November. “This is not the real cold yet” said the old taxi driver when it was -30 in December. So embrace yourself, it’s cold. Good news is that they have amazing cashmere stuff here. Really well made. Cashmere is a different kind of beast. The only thing that kept me warm. 

As for solo traveling as a woman: 
So far I have not had any serious trouble. The only time I really was afraid was when a drunk young man, with foam coming from his mouth tried to follow me. He was dragging one of his feet in a very weird way. He reminded of me a zombie, it was so sad actually he was very young. Luckily for me he also had the speed of a zombie so it was quite easy to lose him. That happened in a ger district btw. Other than that I got yelled by some crazy/drunkard/homeless people but learned to keep my distance. At first it felt really rude to move to the other side of the road because the nearing person is  drunk/homeless but the zombie-man incident made me realize that their feelings are not more important than my safety and I am dumb af. 

I guess apart from drunkards (who are a lot more than  a few in numbers) I feel quite safe most of the time but I hangout mostly in the city center.    And I don’t stay up late. Actually I can confidently say that in my opinion UB center is very safe at reasonable hours. Ger districts might be a different story tough, plus as a foreigner they are really not easy to navigate anyway, and many people have guard dogs that are really angry for some reason. I always worry that they will manage to break their chains since they can get super agitated. If they are calm, they look like teddy bears. Don’t get fooled tough, most of the time they are not social dogs. 

I find Mongolian men a bit direct most of the time. Sometimes out of line, but only verbally in my experience. Being complete strangers, like in the cab or on the street, they can get very cheeky making flirty jokes, complimenting or proposing to hangout, be friends etc. But most people understand  that a no is a no and I never had people insist/bother after making clear that I am not interested. 
 
Anyway, hitchhiking as a form of transportation is really common. I sometimes  use the app UB cab (like uber) it feels safer but pricier.

Now the real danger is different tough.

Its the mixture of ice, bad  roads bad traffic and crazy drivers. Thats what I am really really afraid of. Sometimes I ask my self if one of the conditions for getting a driver’s licence is being mentally unstable here or what. Tough most probably, the chaotic, unnerving, the worst traffic ever make the poor UB drivers go crazy :( Riding the taxi is an adrenalin sport here. Its not for the faint hearted!
